item.title: The 2 set-and-forget Docker containers that do 90% of the heavy lifting in my homelab
item.itunes:title: The 2 set-and-forget Docker containers that do 90% of the heavy lifting in my homelab
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I have installed plenty of Docker containers that looked exciting for a week and then quietly disappeared from my routine. The two I value most are the complete opposite.

One quietly runs much of my smart home, while the other keeps my network cleaner without requiring constant attention. Together, both Home Assistant and Pi-hole probably handle 90% of what I want from my homelab.

My Synology NAS became a home lab centerpiece with these 7 Docker containers

Synology's NAS can be transformed with a few Docker containers.

3
By  Rich Edmonds

Pi-hole

My network’s silent cleanup crew

Pi-hole is one of those services that sounds boring until I actually remove it from my setup. Then I notice the difference almost immediately.

In simple terms, Pi-hole acts as a network-wide DNS filter. Instead of installing ad blockers on every browser and device I own, I can handle much of that filtering in one place. My phones, laptops, tablets, smart TVs, and other connected devices all benefit from the same setup. That alone makes it one of the most useful containers running in my homelab.

What I like even more is how little attention it needs once everything is configured. I point my network to Pi-hole, add the blocklists I want, make a few tweaks, and leave it running.

From there, it quietly blocks unwanted domains, trackers, and plenty of annoying requests in the background. I don’t have to keep opening the dashboard every day or constantly adjust settings to get value from it.

That said, the dashboard is excellent when I do need it. Pi-hole gives me a clean overview of DNS queries, block requests, top clients, frequently requested domains, and more. I can quickly see which device is making the most requests or spot something unusual on my network. The interface is easy to use and understand.

I also like having control over exactly what gets blocked. If Pi-hole breaks something, I can whitelist the domain. If I find another annoying tracker, I can blacklist it. I can also group devices and apply different rules depending on what I want. That flexibility is useful when I have so many different gadgets connected to my network.

This is why I consider Pi-hole one of the containers doing the real heavy lifting in my homelab. It is not something I open because I want to use a cool self-hosted app. It sits underneath everything else and improves the experience across my entire network without reminding me that it is there.

9 Docker containers that run 24/7 on my $100 mini PC

Maximum value budget homelab.

18
By  Samir Makwana

Home Assistant

The brain behind my smart home

Home Assistant is the other container that earns its place in my homelab every single day. The biggest reason I rely on it is simple: I don’t want my smart home split across five different apps.

It works with thousands of services, devices, and companies, which makes it easier to connect the different parts of my smart home without being locked into one ecosystem.

Lights in one app, plugs in another, sensors somewhere else, and routines buried in yet another service quickly become annoying. Home Assistant brings everything into one place. Once I connect my devices and services, I can control most of my smart home from a single dashboard.

I like Home Assistant’s interface. I can create dashboards for different rooms, keep my most-used controls on the main screen, and glance at things like lights, temperature, sensors, switches, and other devices without digging through menus.

Home Assistant is also quite customizable. I am not stuck with whatever interface a smart-home brand wants me to use.

But automations are where Home Assistant really starts doing the heavy lifting. I can build rules once and let Home Assistant handle them. For instance, I can turn lights on at a specific time, switch devices off when nobody is home, trigger actions when a sensor changes, or build routines that involve several devices at once.

These automations take some time to set up, but after that, I stop thinking about them altogether.

I also appreciate how much visibility it gives me. I can check device states, look at history, monitor sensors, and quickly figure out what happened when something does not behave as expected. That makes troubleshooting much easier than jumping between several manufacturer apps.

Another major advantage is the Home Assistant community. It is large, active, and constantly contributing integrations, guides, ideas, and troubleshooting help.

Two services I never touch

The deeper I get into self-hosting, the more convinced I am that most homelabs are overbuilt. More containers, dashboards, and automation do not automatically make a setup better; often, they create more things to babysit.

Home Assistant and Pi-hole easily clear that bar. They solve problems I actually care about and keep earning their place without demanding much in return. They are not the flashiest services I run, but they are easily the ones doing the most work.

item.title: Plex urges users to update after patching serious security flaws
item.itunes:title: Plex urges users to update after patching serious security flaws
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Plex is asking users to install version 1.43.3 of its server and version 1.115.0 of its desktop app to patch undisclosed security flaws.
  • Plex has emailed affected users; NAS owners might need to install updates manually.
  • A 2025 high-severity authentication bug exposed admin tokens.

Plex is asking users to update both their app and media server after releasing an update that patches several security flaws.

The fixes are available in Plex Media Server 1.43.3 (released on May 19th) and Plex Desktop 1.115.0 (released on August 13th). Both updates can be downloaded from Plex's official downloads page. Surprisingly, the self-hosted streaming platform hasn't revealed what those security issues actually were. Plex even went so far as to email users running affected versions of Plex's media server and desktop app.

"We recommend all server owners and Desktop users update to the latest version as soon as possible," writes Plex in an announcement from earlier this week. "If you're running Plex Media Server on a NAS device, the updated version may not be available in their package manager yet, but you can install the package manually."

This isn't the first time Plex has uncovered a notable vulnerability

The streaming app recently rolled back major design changes with its streaming device app

According to The Hacker News, in August 2025, Plex addressed a high-severity security flaw related to an authentication bug stemming from the "'/myplex/account' endpoint incorrectly exposing the server owner's account details, including their administrative access token, even when accessed by any authenticated non-owner or lower-privileged user."

In other Plex-related news, the self-hosted media streaming app recently brought back the collapsible side navigation panel UI with its Apple TV, Roku, Android TV, and Fire TV app. Additionally, a few months ago, the platform raised the price of its popular lifetime Plex Pass from $250 to $750, prompting an uproar from longtime users.

Plex paywalled the features I need, so I started using Jellyfin alongside it

Plex is fine, but too many features are behind a paywall, so I also run started running Jellyfin.

item.title: Even a decade later, the GTX 1080 Ti isn't an easy card to replace
item.itunes:title: Even a decade later, the GTX 1080 Ti isn't an easy card to replace
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
There are very few graphics cards that evoke as much emotion as the iconic GTX 1080 Ti, at least in recent memory. Considering the disappointing gen-on-gen innovation we've seen in the modern GPU market, the GTX 1080 Ti's contrasting history becomes even harder to ignore. It came, it conquered, and it made lifelong loyalists.

It's no wonder many gamers still can't part ways with this card. After all, there's no reason to do that if it still delivers the performance they want. And, surprisingly, it does exactly that in many modern games. For gamers who don't care about ray tracing, high-resolution gaming, or triple-digit framerates, the GTX 1080 Ti is still good enough.

5 old GPUs that are still worth buying used for a budget or retro gaming PC

Skip overpriced new GPUs for highly affordable pre-owned cards

13
By  Tanveer Singh

By most standards, the Pascal flagship is obsolete

That's not breaking news

  • Credit: Nvidia
  • Credit: Remedy Entertainment
  • Credit: Nvidia
  • Credit: Remedy Entertainment

A graphics card becomes objectively obsolete when it fails to stand toe-to-toe with modern equivalents in several key areas. If you look at the GTX 1080 Ti's feature set in 2026, it's hard to argue in its favor. Firstly, there is no hardware ray tracing support here, since real-time ray tracing arrived only on the RTX 20 series cards. Then, there's the lack of DLSS support, so Nvidia's high-quality upscaling and frame generation are absent, too.

The Pascal generation also doesn't support mesh shaders, so modern titles like Alan Wake 2 run terribly on the GTX 1080 Ti. Resizable BAR isn't a thing on these cards, since you need at least an RTX 30 series GPU for that. Lastly, Nvidia ended Game Ready driver support for Pascal cards in October 2025, so the GTX 1080 Ti is on its own, performance-wise.

With so many pieces of the modern gaming pipeline missing from the Pascal flagship, it's easy to grasp its obsolescence. After all, it's been almost a decade since it launched, so we shouldn't be too harsh on it. That being said, there are real reasons why gamers still refuse to upgrade this monster of a card.

Is it just me or was the GTX 10 series the last great generation from Nvidia?

I feel like Nvidia peaked with the GTX 10 series GPUs, all things considered

7
By  Tanveer Singh

But most owners don't see a reason to upgrade yet

Don't fix what ain't broke

  • Credit: Flickr
  • Credit: Flickr

It's a common saying in PC gaming that "your GPU is old only when it stops delivering the performance you want." Fortunately, the GTX 1080 Ti is still pretty capable of 1080p 60+ FPS gaming, at least in most modern titles. Whether it's Cyberpunk 2077, Ghost of Tsushima, Dying Light 2 Stay Human, or Dead Space (2023), breaking the 60 FPS barrier isn't hard for the Pascal flagship, once you adjust the graphics settings.

What's amazing is that the GTX 1080 Ti can even deliver playable framerates in some RT titles, such as Metro Exodus, Battlefield V, Control and Watch Dogs: Legion, although it drops to a 30–40 FPS experience in some of them.

It's basically an RTX 3060 in terms of rasterized performance, and the Ampere card just happens to be one of the most popular GPUs on the Steam Hardware Survey. So, the GTX 1080 Ti isn't going away anytime soon. Not everyone wants to play ray-traced titles with maxed-out settings every day. People still love their lightweight side-scrollers, strategy titles, old classics, and online multiplayer shooters. The GTX 1080 Ti is still enough for that.

It doesn't have DLSS, but FSR upscaling and frame generation are still possible on the Pascal card. Plus, you can use tools like Lossless Scaling and OptiScaler to add these unsupported features to your GTX 1080 Ti. The results vary by the game, but these workarounds have extended the Pascal flagship's life considerably.

5 reasons DLSS and FSR are game-changers for budget gaming PCs

Budget gaming PCs deal with aa ton of constraints. DLSS and FSR help ease the load

2
By  Tanveer Singh

The 11GB VRAM makes the upgrade even harder

Getting enough VRAM today is too much to ask

Another aspect of the GTX 1080 Ti that makes it hard to replace is its VRAM capacity. The 11GB framebuffer makes it serviceable even at 1440p in some modern titles. Where many modern GPUs with 8GB of VRAM turn into a stuttering mess at higher resolutions, the GTX 1080 Ti at least has some headroom to keep going.

Newer-gen cards don't make it cheap for people who want 12GB of VRAM or more. Gamers looking for a high-end upgrade over the GTX 1080 Ti will have to spend over a grand for an 80-class card. And those are just the MSRPs, which have become meaningless in this economy. Memory costs have made everything significantly more expensive, and GPUs are not immune either.

Plus, people need to consider the cost of upgrading everything else around the GPU. A GTX 1080 Ti build is probably quite old by now, so someone upgrading their GPU will also want to switch to a modern platform. This entails buying a new CPU, motherboard, and memory kit, which can quickly ruin all your upgrade plans when you look at DDR5 RAM prices.

The GTX 1080 Ti was just too good. It was an anomaly from Nvidia, and the company hasn't been able to offer anything close, at the right price, to make most owners consider a switch.

$1355 at Amazon
13 years later, the GTX Titan is still the most important GPU Nvidia ever made

Borrowing a $7,000 Tesla and selling it for $1,000 changed everything

3
By  Samarveer Singh

Will Nvidia ever make another GTX 1080 Ti?

The Pascal generation followed the already excellent GTX 900 series, but delivered a massive performance uplift, especially with the GTX 1080 Ti. We've seen similar or bigger jumps after that, but the price-to-performance of the GTX 1080 Ti hasn't really been matched since. The company doesn't need to do that, considering there is no high-end competition, and PC gaming has become a footnote on its balance sheets.

Considering the disappointing gen-on-gen innovation we've seen in the modern GPU market, the GTX 1080 Ti's contrasting history becomes even harder to ignore. It came, it conquered, and it made lifelong loyalists.

It's no wonder many gamers still can't part ways with this card. After all, there's no reason to do that if it still delivers the performance they want. And, surprisingly, it does exactly that in many modern games. For gamers who don't care about ray tracing, high-resolution gaming, or triple-digit framerates, the GTX 1080 Ti is still good enough.

Skip overpriced new GPUs for highly affordable pre-owned cards

By most standards, the Pascal flagship is obsolete

That's not breaking news

A graphics card becomes objectively obsolete when it fails to stand toe-to-toe with modern equivalents in several key areas. If you look at the GTX 1080 Ti's feature set in 2026, it's hard to argue in its favor. Firstly, there is no hardware ray tracing support here, since real-time ray tracing arrived only on the RTX 20 series cards. Then, there's the lack of DLSS support, so Nvidia's high-quality upscaling and frame generation are absent, too.

Another aspect of the GTX 1080 Ti that makes it hard to replace is its VRAM capacity. The 11GB framebuffer makes it serviceable even at 1440p in some modern titles. item.title: My old monitor was collecting dust, so I turned it into a capable smart TV
item.itunes:title: My old monitor was collecting dust, so I turned it into a capable smart TV
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
A few years ago, I purchased a new monitor. It was a couple of years after the release of the Xbox Series X and PlayStation 5, and I was very into Halo Infinite at the time, so I figured it was time to upgrade to a 4K/120Hz capable monitor. I landed on LG's 24-inch UltraGear 27GP950 because it was one of the few monitors at the time that supported 4K and 120Hz (this is way more common now).This meant that my 32-inch Benq EW3280U 4K HDR monitor would be relegated to my crawlspace. Then I remembered I'd been thinking about buying a small TV for my bedroom and realized that instead of turning my very capable Benq monitor into a pricey dust collector, I could repurpose it as a reasonably sized bedroom TV.

This made even more sense given that 32-inch TVs are pretty uncommon these days, and I have no interest in putting a giant 55-inch to 64-inch TV in my small bedroom. Also, who doesn't like saving a bit of money?

Using a monitor as a TV is very easy

Just plug a streaming device into the HDMI port

Along with DisplayPort, most monitors feature at least a few HDMI ports and sometimes even a 3.5mm headphone jack. In my case, I had an extra Apple TV 4K sitting around, so I hooked it up to the Benq EW3280U's HDMI 1 port, and I was mostly up and running right away. You can also use pretty much any HDMI streaming device with your monitor, whether it's a Fire TV Stick, a Roku streaming device, or even something from Walmart's Onn brand — pretty much everything should work.

That said, you need to make sure your monitor is compatible with High-Bandwidth Digital Copy Protection (HDCP), or you might not be able to stream copy-protected content from apps like Netflix and Disney+. Most relatively recent monitors should support this feature, but it's possible it won't if it's older and from the 2000s DVI port era. In this case, your monitor might only support HDCP 1.3, not HDCP 2.2/2.3, so 4K TV shows and movies might not play at full resolution.

If you encounter HDCP issues, using a self-hosted streaming app like Plex or Jellyfin is a great way to work around potential copy protection issues. One odd problem I've encountered is that HDR content doesn't display properly on my Benq EW3280U when I'm streaming TV shows and movies with my Apple TV 4K. For some reason, the picture fades in and out ever so slightly when I turn HDR on, and nothing seems to fix the issue. I've tried 4:4:4 and 4:2:0 chroma settings, but nothing seemed to solve the problem, so I just turned HDR off.

It's a good idea to spend a bit of time tweaking your monitor's display settings. In my case, I needed to increase the brightness better to optimize the picture for darker TV shows and movies. Some monitors will have different display modes optimized for specific kinds of content, similar to standard TVs.

Don't use old HDMI cables with your new TV or monitor

If you're planning to take advantage of high-end features like 120Hz, HDR, and 4K, it's worth making sure you're using the right HDMI cable.

4
By  Patrick O'Rourke

Audio might be a problem

If your monitor doesn't feature built-in speakers, things get a bit more complicated

My Benq EW3280U features built-in speakers, so audio worked instantly, but a display with its own speakers is pretty rare, especially if it's several years old. If that's the case, you still have several audio options. The easiest way is to plug a set of computer speakers into your monitor's 3.5mm headphone jack. This is a quick and cost-effective solution, and you can often find a set of decent computer speakers for $20-30 on Amazon.

If you're using a streaming device like the Apple TV 4K, you can output sound directly to a HomePod mini. Google offers similar functionality with its Google TV Streamer and its new Google Home Speaker. Some streaming devices also work with Bluetooth speakers, allowing you to connect something like a UE Boom to them. If your streamer supports Bluetooth, headphones or earbuds are also an option. Of course, if you're planning to watch TV with other people, this likely isn't the route you'll want to take.

Alternatively, if you're planning to use a higher-end audio setup with your monitor, like a soundbar or a more traditional surround sound setup, you could add an HDMI Audio Extractor. This adapter is useful if your monitor doesn't have a 3.5mm headphone jack or built-in speakers, since it offers a wide variety of inputs, including RCA and optical.

Repurposing old tech is never a bad idea

Whether using a monitor as a TV will work for you ultimately depends on where you plan to set it up. In my case, I wanted a small display in my bedroom, and the 32-inch Benq EW3280U is perfect for that. A monitor could also work well if you want a small TV in your kitchen or your child's bedroom. However, if you're after a full-fledged living room or basement TV replacement, a monitor likely isn't your best bet, especially if it's well under 32-inches.

I like almost everything about the Pixel 11 Pro, but Google played it way too safe

There just really isn't much new this year.

item.title: Picking the wrong Raspberry Pi OS will kill your first project faster than bad hardware ever could
item.itunes:title: Picking the wrong Raspberry Pi OS will kill your first project faster than bad hardware ever could
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The Raspberry Pi is undoubtedly the most interesting piece of tech I've ever heard about. It's small yet fully functional and can work with other sensors and devices to build IoT and automation projects. Even if you don't want to use its GPIO capabilities, you can use the top-end models like the Raspberry Pi 5 as a PC. Other use cases obviously fall into the self-hosted department, where there is a plethora of options to build a useful server. But even before you embark on the self-hosted journey, the first choice you must make is the operating system.

Like every computer, the Raspberry Pi needs an OS to let you interact with it. While distribution variety is a good thing, it's one of the reasons many users cannot make it past their first project. The wrong OS choice can push you into deep problems, and I want you to avoid that.

Operating system abundance is a good thing

But choices become difficult

A quick web search for the best Raspberry Pi OS shows numerous suggestions but no concrete answer. Raspberry Pi operating systems vary with the use case, and you might see the Raspberry Pi OS desktop edition as an obvious choice. It's also one of the closest things you can get to a desktop experience, especially if you are a newbie. You can also choose pure CLI operating systems with no desktop, along with popular options like Ubuntu and a few others.

Then there are niche use-case options, like LibreELEC to turn the Raspberry Pi into a media streaming server, or RetroPie to turn the SBC into a retro game emulation machine. I have not yet discussed other distros, like moOde Audio OS, that convert your Pi into a streaming server. I used it to revive an old speaker system, and now it has Bluetooth connectivity with speakers.

Incorrect OS selection can ruin your experience

Complex OS editions

After being dazed by so many options, you begin to consider installing the official Raspberry Pi OS with a desktop, because it seems like an obvious choice. Rather than learning to navigate the terminal, you get a simple head start with an OS that resembles your regular computer workflow. It has a desktop with icons and menus, and basic tasks like enabling an internet connection and setting up apps via a built-in package installer look promising. But it won't work with every Raspberry Pi model.

So what's the option? Use a CLI OS like the Raspberry Pi OS Lite or Ubuntu Server, both of which lack a desktop environment. That's a mistake I made on my Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, after I switched to the CLI version of the official OS. Suddenly, I was staring at a blank terminal with bare-minimum configuration options, and when I started installing packages, errors popped up like crazy. A syntax issue, lack of permissions, incorrect directory, and whatnot.

The best Raspberry Pi projects don’t require extra hardware anymore

You don't need to spend a fortune on premium Raspberry Pi HATs and gizmos for your DIY projects

2
By  Ayush Pande

I might sound biased with my suggestion, but I regret not picking DietPi as my first Raspberry Pi OS. While it's a CLI OS like Ubuntu and the official one, it gives beginners much more breathing room. DietPi puts more effort into being an easy-going OS with built-in tools, a dedicated software installation option, and a nice CLI dashboard with all the useful information. DietPi puts thought into the basic actions that can be a problem for someone new to SBCs.

Its whiptail menus make it feel like a regular OS with interactive apps. You have to navigate them with a keyboard, but it's so much better than the terminal. But if you go with something like Ubuntu Server or the official offerings, every action requires a command. Be it adding a USB drive, mounting it, assigning user permissions, installing packages, or controlling services.

Matching usability with resource requirements

An operating system should complement the hardware

Performance problems can show up if you pick the wrong OS. For example, the official Raspberry Pi OS desktop edition can work comfortably on something like the Raspberry Pi 5 or 4B, but becomes a pain for the Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. Even the 32-bit version of the desktop edition brings the Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W to its knees, as the 512MB of memory cannot keep up with the demands of a graphical environment.

When choosing an OS for your SBC, focus on its resource requirements. Carefully evaluate what it needs and whether your SBC has enough hardware resources to meet the target. It’s crucial because after installing the OS, the Raspberry Pi should have enough left to run your tools like Docker or even independent packages. So, DietPi is a great choice for a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, while Raspberry Pi OS Desktop runs nicely on the Raspberry Pi 4B with 4GB RAM. I prefer a lean approach, and DietPi lets me achieve that with the basic terminal knowledge I possess.

3 things I wish I knew about the Raspberry Pi before I bought one

Raspberry Pis are great, but they're tricky to get into.

By  Simon Batt

You can go for an OS with a desktop environment if you find remote SSH cumbersome and prefer a GUI to configure the system and fix issues. If you want to free up maximum resources, you have to pick a CLI OS. But there’s even a solution like DietPi that makes the process less arduous. Similarly, you can pivot to a desktop experience on DietPi or other CLI distros by installing a lightweight desktop environment like XFCE. I’ve experimented with most of them, and I picked DietPi because I want to squeeze out every bit of performance I can.

Choose wisely

Focus on an OS that provides a solid base and is minimally complex. A slightly advanced user will focus on performance more because troubleshooting isn’t a problem. But if you are completely new to self-hosting, a desktop-based OS or something like DietPi (both of which have good software support) should be a priority. Estimate the amount of free system resources you’ll be left with after installing the OS, and whether the SBC hardware can actually run it without stutters.

Raspberry Pi 5
CPU
Arm Cortex-A76 (quad-core, 2.4GHz)
Memory
Up to 8GB LPDDR4X SDRAM

The Raspberry Pi is back, and the fifth iteration of the SBC is a lot more capable than the older models. From a new quad-core Arm Cortex-A76 CPU, support for dual monitor setups at 4K 60Hz, and a dedicated power button, there's a lot to love about this palm-sized computer.

item.title: This tiny PowerToys feature fixed one of my biggest Windows multitasking annoyances
item.itunes:title: This tiny PowerToys feature fixed one of my biggest Windows multitasking annoyances
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've been using a triple-monitor setup for the last four years, and at this point, I can't imagine going back to two monitors, let alone just one. My current setup gives me plenty of screen space to work with, especially since one of them is ultrawide. Whether I'm writing for XDA, looking at stocks in TradingView, or just keeping a bunch of apps open while researching, I rarely feel like I'm running out of space.

Still, that wasn't enough to address one of the main problems I face while multitasking in Windows. There are times when I want to keep a particular window visible while I'm working in another app, but the moment I click on that app, the window I wanted to stay visible gets buried behind it. Of course, with the amount of space I have, I can rearrange my windows, but that feels unnecessary when I only need it there temporarily. That's exactly why I started using Always On Top in PowerToys, and now multitasking is so much more convenient.

Windows PowerToys' Always On Top finally clicked when I realized I could pin multiple apps at once

Always On Top felt basic until I discovered that I could pin multiple apps at once and keep my reference windows from disappearing.

By  Judy Sanhz

Always On Top is the multitasking fix I needed

One keyboard shortcut to stop windows from getting buried

As the name already suggests, Always On Top lets you pin a window so that it stays above everything else on your screen. You can click on anything else around this window, and it won't budge. Once you've enabled it in PowerToys, click the window you want to keep visible and press its keyboard shortcut, which is Win + Ctrl + T by default. You'll see a colored border around this pinned window to let you know it's set to stay on top. And whenever you want to unpin it, select that window and press the same shortcut again.

That's pretty much all you need to learn to get started with Always On Top. I personally use it for those short stretches where I need to reference something without repeatedly digging it back out of the taskbar. For example, if I need to compare specs while writing, I just open a separate window and keep it pinned in a corner. The same goes when I want to keep an eye on a stock in TradingView or do quick math in the Calculator app. It's such a simple feature, but it has become one of the main reasons why I still have PowerToys installed.

This is better than rearranging my entire desktop

The last thing I want is a temporary window to ruin my layout

Since I have three monitors, you're probably thinking it's better to drag the window I need over to another screen. But here's the thing. I already have at least one window open on all three monitors most of the time, and I arrange them exactly how I like so I don't have to twist my head around. Making room for another window means resizing something or using FancyZones to reorganize my desktop. I find that a bit overkill when I only need that tiny window for a few minutes.

Yes, using Always On Top does mean the pinned window will hide whatever is directly behind it, but that hasn't really bothered me so far. I usually move it to a corner on my ultrawide monitor, so it rarely ever gets in the way. If that's a dealbreaker for you, you can adjust the opacity of the pinned windows in Always On Top's settings. You can also reduce the border thickness or disable it completely. I've made it thinner just so I know it's active. And lastly, if you find the keyboard shortcut a bit awkward, you can enable the option to access Always On Top from the title bar's context menu as well.

I'd avoid overusing it, though

Having three or four windows pinned on top can get overwhelming

When I first tried out this feature, I liked it so much that I started pinning pretty much every small window I opened. That quickly became overwhelming because I'd have three or four windows sitting above the main window at the same time. The problem here is that I'd have to unpin them one by one when I no longer need them, which feels like more work than simply dragging windows around. At that point, I'd argue Always On Top adds more clutter than it helps me multitask.

However, when you use it sparingly and are selective about the windows you want to pin, Always On Top feels like a feature that should've been built into Windows from the start. These days, I stick to pinning one window at a time, and lean on FancyZones whenever I want several windows visible at once. This way, I still get the convenience without turning my desktop into a mess. All in all, Always On Top works incredibly well as long as you know when to avoid it.

This is just scratching the surface of PowerToys

Always On Top isn't even the standout feature of PowerToys. I first installed it for Command Palette and FancyZones, only to find myself using Always On Top almost every time I'm working or gaming on my PC. That's why I'd recommend checking everything else it has to offer instead of just using Always On Top and calling it a day. For me, this little tool fixed a problem three monitors couldn't, but for you, it might be something else entirely.

item.title: Your guest network is probably faster than your main network, and it's because you optimized it to death
item.itunes:title: Your guest network is probably faster than your main network, and it's because you optimized it to death
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Even if you spent thousands of dollars on prosumer networking gear, sometimes your throwaway guest network can run laps around your primary SSID, and this will feel like a personal failure. It's not always an RF issue, like channel interference or bad MIMO spatial streaming. It might actually be down to the mountain of prosumer optimizations you stacked on over the years, from inline deep packet inspection and double DNS syncs to policy-based VPN gateways and unaccelerated CPU software bridges.

The guest network was faster simply because it was untouched, hardware-offloaded raw routing. In modern networking, every Layer 7 security feature, DNS inspection hop, and traffic shaping rule extracts a measurable CPU and latency tax. This means, with a significantly over-engineered primary network, you're turning your high-end router into a congested bottleneck, proving that the clearest path to multi-gig speeds is knowing which features to leave off.

My old switch has a feature I ignored for years, and it fixed my home network

I regret ignoring my switch's loop detection provisions for years

13
By  Ayush Pande

What causes your network to fall apart?

There is a range of different choke points

Four main hidden packet choke points can slow your main network, and understanding these technical mechanics may let you fix the issue.

Deep packet inspection: On your primary LAN, you turned on IDS/IPS level 5, meaning everything is being inspected. Every single packet payload traversing your router CPU undergoes stateful pattern matching against thousands of signature rules. Because consumer and prosumer router CPUs lack high-end enterprise ACI packet accelerators enabling IPS, IPS disables hardware offloading and bottlenecks maximum throughput from 1 Gbps down to 300 to 400 Mbps. For your guest network, most firewalls exclude guest VLANs from packet inspection by default to save CPU cycles, so traffic doesn't have to go through all of this and can connect faster.

The double DNS resolver chain can be another issue. If the DNS cache misses or your self-hosted DNS container is bogged down with regenerating and logging, then the time to first byte for initial connection handshakes adds 50 to 100ms of lag per web request. Your guest network, on the other hand, usually hands out ISP or public DNS via DHCP, executing lookups in under 10ms with zero local container hops.

If you set up policy-based routing that routes your entire main subnet through a commercial VPE gateway or an encrypted cloud tunnel for privacy, this can cause major issues too. The router CPU chokes on constant cryptographic encryption/decryption overhead at line speed.

When you enable software traffic shaping on high-bandwidth links without dedicated multi-core silicon, the Linux kernel must disable hardware flow offloading. This means the guest network, operating without complex QoS policies, bypasses the Linux network stack software queue and hits Silicon Novel hardware switching, so it doesn't face the repercussions.

How to run a diagnostic audit

It's time to pinpoint the issue

Since so many factors could be causing issues with your main LAN, you can hone in and find out exactly what is causing the problems. In order to do this, you need to run a diagnostic audit. By running through this checklist, you can audit each component of your network gear.

Run an iperf3 test between a Wi-Fi laptop and a hardwired local 10G/2.5G server. If local throughput hits 800+ Mbps, the Wi-Fi access point and radio frequency spectrum are just fine. The bottleneck is strictly inside the router's WAN gateway and packet engine. If your local throughput isn't reaching these speeds, it may be time to relocate your router and optimize the RF spectrum.

The next test you can undertake is checking your CPU load during a WAN speed test. SSH into your gateway and run `htop` or `top` while running an external speed test. If a single core pegs at 100% utilization, which is often consumed by something like a VPN, then you've identified your software bottleneck.

You can also audit hardware offloading flags. You can verify whether hardware flow offloading or cut-through forwarding is disabled by going to Settings -> Security -> General -> Suspicious Activity. Check if IPS throughput exceeds your ISP tier. If it does, then switch this off or adjust as necessary.

It might be time to start from scratch

You might have overdone it

Many of the features you've implemented over the years are likely for security, but luckily there is a way to keep your security without killing your speeds. If you feel like you want to start from scratch and reconfigure your network to ensure that you can have the best of both worlds, then here's a list of how to re-architect your main network. This should result in it matching your guest network's performance without you having to abandon any of your home lab control.

Modernize your DNS. Run AdGuard Home on dedicated bare-metal hardware, not inside an overloaded VM sharing router CPU cores. Tune DNS cache sizes and enable optimistic caching.

Scope IDS/IPS exclusively to exposed ports. There's no point inspecting outbound Netflix, Steam, and Speed Test streams. Configure your intrusion detection system to inspect only inbound WAN traffic targeting exposed reverse proxies or hosted ports only. This way you're not wasting CPU cycles scanning packets that just don't need to be scanned.

Make sure you also have the right-sized QoS for high-speed lanes. If your internet connection is above 500Mbps, traditional CPU-bound SQM algorithms often introduce more latency and throughput penalties than they fix. Disable SQM on multi-gig connections unless bufferbloat is causing packet drops.

Use dedicated WireGuard hardware acceleration. You can offload VPN routing to devices with native hardware crypto instructions or use split tunneling so bulk downloads and streams bypass the VPN altogether.

Over-configuration might be an issue

Bring down the engineering

Building a home lab teaches you that more dials and toggles do not automatically equal a better network. The guest network wasn't fast because of some secret engineering triumph. It was fast because it did what a network was originally designed to do: move packets from A to B with the minimum interference. Over-engineering a network can be fatal.

Run a speed test on your guest network today. If it embarrasses your primary setup, don't buy a new router. Open your gateway dashboard, turn off the features you don't actually need, and let your silicon breathe.

item.title: Please stop using your ISP's DNS
item.itunes:title: Please stop using your ISP's DNS
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The internet can be a pretty scary place, and while we use privacy-focused browsers, know what phishing attempts look like, and use password managers to keep our secrets safe, another piece of information gets siphoned off every time you navigate to a new webpage. At least, if you're still using the DNS servers that your ISP or cellular provider set up when you first got service, because those plaintext queries get stored and sold to advertisers and anyone else who might want to get their hands on the information they hold.

If you care about your online privacy, it's time to stop using your ISP's DNS servers. You don't have to self-host a DNS server if you don't want to, but take a little time to research an external DNS provider that uses encrypted methods, and switch to that on all your devices. Every little piece of data you can claw back from your ISP and other data hogs is worth the effort.

The problem with your ISP's DNS

Okay, problems, plural, because they're not your friend

There are many reasons you'd not want your ISP resolving your DNS queries, but most of them boil down to one thing — privacy. ISPs are lousy at this, whether it's not enabling DNSSEC to ensure DNS responses are authentic and untampered with, or bundling your browsing habits into nice packages to sell to advertisers as supposedly anonymous data. In a world where all data is for sale, sending out unencrypted DNS records is another way for you and your habits to be tracked.

The other thing that your ISP does is network-level DNS blocks of any resources or websites that they deem unsafe, potentially cutting off access to chunks of the open internet. That could be a good thing, if they're blocking known malware sources, but it doesn't take much of an imagination to see it potentially used for blocking adult content, tools for video game preservation, or anything that the ISP decides to block (or gets a legal notice from the government to do so).

By moving to another DNS provider, you sidestep any ISP-level blocks. It doesn't guaranteed your new DNS provider doesn't have its own blocks, but these are generally more forthcoming about what and why they're blocking certain content, and it's mostly for the user's benefit and safety.

You don't have to self-host DNS

Many of the commercial alternatives are safe and secure

There are plenty of private DNS providers worldwide to get encrypted DNS set up with the minimum of fuss. You don't have to self-host anything to use these options; instead you change the DNS server on every device you want to use it on, from your router to smartphones and more. That gives your devices better security, circumvents any ISP-level blocks to DNS resolution, and helps you stay more private when online.

While encrypted DNS will keep your ISP from seeing your DNS queries, it's not going to keep your browsing private. You'll need a VPN or other securely encrypted method of accessing the internet for that.

You'll want to make sure the DNS provider you choose supports DNSSEC, QNAME Minimization, and also either disable or anonymize EDNS Client Subnet (ECS) if it's available. Also, you don't want it to log personal data to disk, and it should support anycast or geo-steering.

In no particular order, each of these DNS providers will be more secure and private than your ISP's:

  • Cloudflare (1.1.1.1): Runs a large chunk of the internet, known for not blocking sites unless known as a threat
  • Quad9 (9.9.9.9): Encrypted DNS, also known for not blocking sites without them serving malware or other threats
  • Control D (76.76.2.2): No logging, various encryption methods, and works on Apple devices
  • AdGuard Public DNS: Anonymized, uses some filtering, has Apple profiles.

These should all also support various encrypted options, including DNS-over-HTTPS, DNS-over-TLS, or DNS-over-Quic. And with how often DNS goes wrong, it's always a good idea to use a trusted DNS solution for the best and most secure option.

But self-hosting gives you more control

You get ad-blocking, locally resolved domains, and more

Self-hosting a DNS server is deceptively simple to do these days, whether you choose from any of the options, including Unbound, AdGuard Home, PowerDNS, or my personal favorite, Technitium. You'll still want to have some queries sent to an external DNS server in an encrypted manner for fallback, but having your own local DNS server making its own encrypted requests will increase the security and privacy of your home network and the devices using that DNS server.

You get all the bonuses of using an existing DNS provider, like ad blocking at the source, plus you can set up zones, split horizon DNS so that different devices on your network get different DNS results, and local domain rebinds, which are very handy for home lab use. Add in dnscrypt-proxy as a local frontend (if needed), and your DNS requests are unreadable by your ISP. Finally, block port 53 to force every device to use your new local DNS server via encrypted egress, and you're in (relative) control over your DNS queries.

Whatever you choose, it's time to stop using your ISP's DNS servers

Using the DNS servers your ISP defaults to might be easy, but it's not good for your online privacy. Plus, your DNS data is likely being sold for advertising use, along with any other data that the ISP can sniff. Using an encrypted DNS provider means your ISP is cut out of the loop, so while it doesn't make your browsing private, it does reduce the exposure of your online usage. And it's not just your browsing habits, because your location can be triangulated with DNS queries, and that's possibly more worrisome.

And it's not just your browsing habits, because your location can be triangulated with DNS queries, and that's possibly more worrisome.

item.itunes:summary:
There are a few alternatives to Microsoft's Office suite out there, and a bit of competition among them. The most popular is, of course, LibreOffice, though I tend to prefer the likes of OnlyOffice.

But for the Linux users out there, there's an Offise suite that no one really talks about, despite having a pretty big name behind it. It's called Calligra, and it's made by the KDE team, responsible for one of my favorite Linux desktop environments, KDE Plasma. With that kind of pedigree, I was surprised it took me so long to find out it even existed. But after trying to use it, I kind of get it.

A native, if convoluted UI

It's not the easiest to use

One of the things that drew me to Calligra is that it's very clearly made as part of the broader KDE suite of apps, using the Qt6 framework for the UI. I'm not necessarily against custom UIs, but I do like when a platform can standardize, and the Calligra apps fall right in line with other KDE software at first glance, which makes it a perfect fit if you're using KDE Plasma.

Office apps are much more convoluted than the usual software KDE makes, though, so there's deifnitely a challenge in bringing these two things together in a way that feels good to use.

Instead of the typical top menu bar or ribbon, Calligra puts most of the formatting tools on the right side of the app window, with only a handful of menus along the top. These can be viewing options for Words, formatting tools in Sheets, or even the ability to switch between a slide and its notes in Stage.

I switched from GNOME to KDE Plasma 6.6 and it fixed all my complaints about the Linux desktop

It's time to move on from GNOME

21
By  João Carrasqueira

This can get confusing, especially in Sheets, where a lot of the tools you'd usually find around the same area are now split between the top menu and the one on the right. It also feels like the menu on the right wastes more space on the screen and reduces the work area, but you can resize this sidebar, so it's not a huge deal.

It does the basics

And not much else

Like most Office-style suites, Calligra offers the basic functionality you'd expect. There are four apps included in the main package: Words, Sheets, Stage, and Karbon.

The first three are the replacements for the features you'd expect, with Stage being the slideshow presentation maker. Karbon is a graphic design tool, which means it's also the app I need the least of the bunch, as well as the one I have the least experience with. It is nice to see these suites go a bit further than just the basics, though.

As far as the basic apps go, things work as you'd expect. Words lets you write up and format documents, though there are no templates I could find, Sheets can in fact create and format spreadsheets, and Stage actually seems like one of the better options, offering the usual array of formatting tools, animations, and even some preset templates that look kind of nice. Sheets can also load up CSV files and format them properly, which is better than I've seen other apps do. I was also able to open files using Microsoft's proprietary formats, and for the basic ones, things looked fine.

But while it gets the basics well enough, things get rough for Calligra as you try to explore more of its features.

I finally found free open-source tools that beat Microsoft Office 365 where it counts

The open-source productivity upgrade I should’ve tried years ago.

7
By  Yash Patel

Too much is missing

Especially in Sheets

As I used Calligra, it didn't take long to realize why this suite doesn't get as much attention as some others. Sheets is easily the biggest offender, because it fails at even one of the most basic aspects: when I load the app, the spreadsheet follows the app's dark theme, except text is still black by default, making the entire thing unreadable.

It gets worse as there's also no proper support for inserting or creating tables in a spreadsheet, and while that's not too surprising (OnlyOffice seems to be the only free option that handles this perfectly), this is easily the worst I've seen it be. Even opening an existing document with a table renders it as if there were no sorting options at all.

5 free Office alternatives for Mac that are better than Apple's

You've already spent enough

2
By  João Carrasqueira

On top of that, Sheets can be quite slow, and it will freeze entirely if you try to format the entire sheet at once. It's basically unusable for the only use case I usually have with spreadsheets.

Words offering no options for templates or dedicated formatting also makes it a problem. Even if you just want to make a nice title page, there just aren't any options to make that easier. You'd have to format everything manually.

I still want to hope

It could be great

Like I've mentioned, the KDE team makes one of my favorite desktops for Linux, and its software is generally incredible, with very strong support from the developers. When I discovered Calligra, I hoped it would be treated the same, but it clearly isn't.

I wanted to highlight Calligra because I do believe there's potential here. KDE has many fans and many contributors, but even a lot of those people don't know Calligra exists, which is probably why updates are infrequent and tiny. The last major update for the suite seems to have been two years ago, and even the official website has little more to share.

11 Linux apps Windows refugees need to know about

Scared of ditching Windows? These Linux apps make things so much easier

25
By  João Carrasqueira

I'd love to see the team put more effort into making Calligra a solid competitor to LibreOffice or OnlyOffice. As it stands, not even KDE's own Linux distro comes with Calligra preinstalled, but that could be a big step in making the app more well-known, which in turn could draw attention from developers to make it better.

I'm hoping that's what happens, but in the meantime, if you want to check it out yourself, you can download Callighra from Flathub or check your distro's repositories if you're looking for a native package.
